However, poor cysticidal activity, chronic conjunctival infection, and resistance to some strains of Acanthamoeba to propa- midine has prompted the suggestion that it should be replaced by another diamidine such as hexamidine. Systemic itraconazole or ketoconazole with topical mi- conazole have also been tried with some success. Clot- rimazole has also been used successfully. Biguanides may also be used alone,4 and are particularly effective in early infection. Acanthamoeba keratitis in contact lens wearers should be preventable by good lens hygiene (see Contact Lens Care, p.1622). 1. Illingworth CD, et al. Acanthamoeba keratitis: risk factors and outcome. Acanthamoeba keratitis update—incidence, molecular epidemiology and new drugs for treatment. Eye 2003; 17: 893–905. DISSEMINATED ACANTHAMOEBA INFECTION. Granulo- matous amoebic encephalitis is caused by infection with free-living amoebae, usually Acanthamoeba spp. or sometimes leptomyxid amoebae. It is an opportunis- tic infection occurring mainly in debilitated or immuno- compromised individuals. The protozoa spread to the CNS from pulmonary or skin lesions and produce focal neurological deficits that progress over days or weeks to a diffuse meningoencephalitis. The infection is usu- ally fatal and most cases have been diagnosed postmor- tem so little is known about effective treatments; A few cases have been reported in which patients with en- cephalitis responded to combinations of pentamidine, sulfadiazine, flucytosine, and an azole such as itracona- zole or fluconazole;1 susceptibilities of species and strains appear to vary widely, and susceptibility testing is advisable. Clinical responses to chemotherapy have also been report- ed in a few patients2-4 with disseminated infection but no evidence of CNS involvement
